options.text: Present all options: expectant, medical (misoprostol), or surgical. Support her decision after informed consent
options.rationale: Missed abortion management includes expectant (1-4 weeks for spontaneous passage), medical (misoprostol), or surgical (D&C). The patient's autonomy should be respected after counseling on risks/benefits of each.
Methotrexate is for ectopic pregnancy, not missed abortion. Misoprostol is the appropriate medical agent for early pregnancy loss.
Surgical evacuation is the most predictable approach but is not mandatory. Expectant and medical management are valid options when the patient is stable.
Ethics committee referral is not needed for standard management of early pregnancy loss. All management options are medically and ethically acceptable.

rationale: Missed abortion: offer all three options (expectant, medical, surgical). Respect patient autonomy while ensuring informed decision-making.

question: A 38-year-old asks about cervical cancer screening. She is healthy, non-smoker, no prior abnormal Paps. What is the most appropriate screening recommendation?

options.text: Pap smear every 3 years starting at age 21, or co-testing (Pap + HPV) every 5 years starting at age 30
options.rationale: Cervical screening: age 21-29: Pap every 3 years. Age 30-65: Pap + HPV co-testing every 5 years or Pap alone every 3 years.
Cervical cancer screening is recommended for all women 21-65 regardless of symptoms. Precancerous lesions are asymptomatic.

options.text: Pap smear every year starting at age 18
options.rationale: Annual screening is not recommended. Screening starts at 21 regardless of sexual activity. Over-screening can lead to unnecessary procedures.

options.text: HPV vaccine only, no Pap needed
options.rationale: HPV vaccine prevents HPV types 16/18 (causing 70% of cervical cancers) but does not eliminate the need for screening as other high-risk types exist.

rationale: Cervical cancer screening: Pap 3-yearly ages 21-29, co-test 5-yearly ages 30-65. Stop at 65 with adequate prior negative screens.

question: A 39-year-old at 20 weeks presents with a 2 cm firm breast mass that she noticed 2 weeks ago. Ultrasound shows a solid, irregular mass. What is the most appropriate diagnostic approach?

options.rationale: Mammogram can be performed safely in pregnancy with abdominal shielding but is adjunctive to ultrasound and biopsy, not a replacement.
MRI with contrast has limited safety data in pregnancy and is not first-line for evaluating breast masses. Ultrasound + biopsy is preferred.
Any suspicious breast mass in pregnancy requires definitive diagnosis without delay. Breast cancer aggressiveness is similar in pregnancy.
A solid, irregular breast mass in pregnancy requires tissue diagnosis. Core needle biopsy is safe during pregnancy and is the gold standard for diagnosis.

rationale: Suspicious breast mass in pregnancy: ultrasound + core needle biopsy. Mammogram with shielding is safe. Cancer treatment depends on gestational age.

question: A 40-year-old primigravida at 34 weeks presents with BP 160/105, proteinuria 3+, and severe headache. Platelets 90, ALT 120, Cr 1.2. What is the most appropriate management?

options.rationale: MgSO4 is for seizure prophylaxis, not treatment of underlying disease. Delivery remains the definitive management.

options.text: Deliver after corticosteroid course if stable
options.rationale: Severe preeclampsia at ≥34 weeks requires delivery. A short course of steroids for fetal lung maturity can be given if maternal and fetal status permit delay.
Severe preeclampsia requires inpatient management with IV antihypertensives and monitoring. Outpatient care is for mild disease only.
Severe preeclampsia with end-organ damage precludes expectant management. Delaying delivery risks eclampsia, hepatic rupture, and maternal death.

rationale: Severe preeclampsia ≥34 weeks: deliver after steroids. MgSO4 for seizure prophylaxis. BP control with labetalol or hydralazine.

question: A 41-year-old at 32 weeks presents with painless bright red vaginal bleeding. No contractions. Fundal height appropriate. What is the most appropriate initial diagnostic step?

options.text: Amniocentesis to assess fetal lung maturity
options.rationale: Amniocentesis has no role in diagnosing the cause of acute third-trimester bleeding and carries procedural risk.
BPP assesses fetal wellbeing but does not diagnose the cause of bleeding. Placental localization is the priority.
Digital exam is contraindicated when previa is suspected due to risk of provoking catastrophic hemorrhage.
Painless third trimester bleeding is placenta previa until proven otherwise. Ultrasound is first-line and safe. Digital exam is contraindicated.

rationale: Painless third trimester bleeding: ultrasound to locate placenta. NO digital exam. If previa confirmed: admit, steroids, deliver at 36-37 weeks if stable.

question: A 42-year-old at 36 weeks presents with sudden severe abdominal pain and dark vaginal bleeding. Uterus is rigid and tender. FHR shows late decelerations. BP 85/50. What is the most appropriate management?

options.rationale: Tocolysis is contraindicated in abruption. Uterine contractions may worsen bleeding and fetal compromise.
Abruption is a clinical diagnosis. Delaying delivery for imaging risks fetal demise.
Abruption with non-reassuring fetal status and maternal hemodynamic instability requires emergency delivery. DIC is a life-threatening complication.
Fetal distress and maternal instability mandate immediate delivery. Expectant management risks fetal death and maternal coagulopathy.

rationale: Abruptio placentae with fetal distress and maternal shock: emergency delivery. Evaluate for DIC and prepare for massive transfusion.

question: A 43-year-old at 30 weeks presents with regular painful contractions and cervical dilation of 3 cm on exam. Membranes intact. Fetal status reassuring. What is the most appropriate management?

options.rationale: Delivery is indicated when tocolysis is contraindicated (chorioamnionitis, severe preeclampsia, non-reassuring fetal status) or labor is too advanced.
Preterm labor at <34 weeks with intact membranes and reassuring fetal status: tocolysis for 48 hours allows corticosteroids to enhance fetal lung maturity.
Preterm labor requires hospitalization for monitoring, tocolysis, and steroid administration. Outpatient management is not appropriate.
Tocolysis buys time for steroids to work (maximal effect at 48 hours). With 3 cm dilation, the patient may deliver before steroids take effect without tocolysis.

rationale: Preterm labor <34 weeks: tocolysis + steroids + GBS prophylaxis. If cervical dilation >6 cm or chorioamnionitis: deliver.

question: A 44-year-old at 36 weeks presents with fluid leaking per vagina for 2 hours. Pooling and ferning are positive on speculum exam. No contractions. Fetal status reassuring. What is the most appropriate management?

options.rationale: There is no surgical method to reseal ruptured membranes. Induction or expectant management are the only options.
PROM at ≥36 weeks: induction of labor is recommended to reduce chorioamnionitis risk. GBS prophylaxis should be given if indicated.
PROM at ≤37 weeks is managed by induction unless very close to term. The risk of ascending infection outweighs benefits of waiting.
Tocolysis is contraindicated in PROM due to infection risk. Delivery is the goal when the cervix is unfavorable and membranes are ruptured at term.

rationale: PROM ≥36 weeks: induction. 34-36 weeks: steroids + induction vs expectant. <34 weeks: steroids + antibiotics + expectant management with monitoring for infection.

question: A 45-year-old delivered vaginally 20 minutes ago. Fundus is boggy and uterus is at the umbilicus. Heavy bright red bleeding continues despite fundal massage. What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacologic management?

options.text: IV oxytocin 10-40 IU in 1 L normal saline
options.rationale: Oxytocin is first-line for uterine atony. It causes sustained uterine contraction. Dose: 10-40 IU in 1 L NS, infused at 125-200 mL/hour.
Misoprostol is third-line and less effective than oxytocin. Used when IV access is limited. Causes fever and shivering.
Carboprost (PGF2α) is second-line when oxytocin fails. Contraindicated in asthma. Effective for atony but causes nausea, vomiting, and bronchospasm.
TXA 1 g IV is adjunctive, given within 3 hours of delivery. It reduces death from bleeding by 20% but does not replace uterotonics.

rationale: PPH: uterine massage + oxytocin first-line. Escalate: ergometrine → carboprost → misoprostol → intrauterine balloon → surgical.

question: A 46-year-old at 28 weeks has a hemoglobin of 10.2 g/dL. MCV 82, ferritin 15. Which physiologic change of pregnancy most likely contributes to this finding?

options.rationale: Pregnancy does not cause hemolysis. A falling hemoglobin with elevated LDH and low haptoglobin would suggest pathologic hemolysis.

options.text: Physiologic hemodilution from plasma volume expansion
options.rationale: Plasma volume increases ~50% while red cell mass increases only ~25%, causing dilutional anemia in the second and third trimesters. This is physiologic, not pathologic.
Fetal iron demands increase in the third trimester, but physiologic hemodilution is the primary cause of lower hemoglobin earlier. Iron studies help distinguish.
Folate deficiency causes macrocytic anemia (high MCV). This patient's MCV is normal, making folate deficiency unlikely.

rationale: Gestational anemia is primarily dilutional. Iron, folate, and B12 should be evaluated. Supplementation is standard regardless.

question: A 47-year-old primigravida at 10 weeks presents for initial prenatal visit. She is healthy with no chronic conditions. What routine lab tests should be ordered at this visit?

options.rationale: Chest X-ray is not a routine prenatal lab. TB screening is indicated only for high-risk populations (exposure, symptoms, high-prevalence country).

options.text: OGTT for gestational diabetes at 10 weeks
options.rationale: OGTT is performed at 24-28 weeks routinely or earlier only if risk factors (prior GDM, BMI >30). Not part of initial visit labs.

options.text: Blood type/Rh, antibody screen, CBC, HIV, syphilis, hepatitis B, rubella titer, urinalysis
options.rationale: Standard first-trimester labs include blood group + antibody screen, CBC, HIV, syphilis, HBsAg, rubella, and urinalysis. These establish baseline and identify risks.
Amniocentesis is offered at 15-20 weeks for women ≥35 or abnormal NIPT/serum screen. Not routine at 10 weeks.

rationale: First prenatal visit: comprehensive history, blood work, urinalysis, dating ultrasound. Supplements: folic acid, iron, vitamin D.

question: A 48-year-old primigravida at 40 weeks presents with contractions every 3 minutes, cervical dilation 6 cm, 100% effaced. FHR is 145 with moderate variability. What stage of labor is this patient in?

options.rationale: Active first stage: 6-10 cm dilation, regular contractions. Nulliparous women dilate ~1 cm/hour. FHR monitoring should be continuous.
Third stage is from delivery of the infant to delivery of the placenta. This patient is still in the active phase of first stage.
Second stage begins at complete dilation (10 cm) and ends with delivery. This patient is not yet fully dilated.
Latent phase: 0-6 cm, slower progress. This patient has passed the latent-to-active transition at 6 cm.

rationale: Active phase (6-10 cm) progresses at ~1 cm/hour for nulliparas. If protraction or arrest occurs, evaluate for augmentation with oxytocin.

question: A 49-year-old G1P1 had a vaginal delivery with second-degree perineal laceration repaired. She is breastfeeding. Which contraceptive method is most appropriate at this postpartum visit?

options.text: Progestin-only pill or IUD (Cu-IUD or LNG-IUS)
options.rationale: Postpartum contraception: progestin-only methods and IUDs are safe during breastfeeding. Progestin-only pills start immediately; IUDs can be placed at 4-6 weeks postpartum.
Natural family planning has high failure rates in the postpartum period due to unpredictable return of ovulation and cycles.
COCs are relatively contraindicated during breastfeeding in the first 3-6 weeks due to potential effects on milk production. Progestin-only methods are preferred.
Tubal ligation is permanent and requires informed consent before or after delivery. It is not the first-line recommendation for a healthy new mother.

rationale: Postpartum contraception: progestin-only methods are safe during breastfeeding. IUDs placed at 4-6 weeks postpartum.

question: A 50-year-old at 39 weeks in active labor has an FHR tracing showing variable decelerations dropping to 70 bpm, lasting 60 seconds, with moderate variability between contractions. What is the most appropriate interpretation?

options.rationale: Category I requires all: baseline 110-160, moderate variability, NO decelerations. Variables make this Category II.
Category III: absent variability + recurrent late/variables, or bradycardia. This has moderate variability, making it Category II.
Fetal scalp sampling is used to clarify indeterminate tracings but is not the first step. Intrauterine resuscitation should be initiated first.

options.text: Category II (indeterminate) — continue monitoring and consider intrauterine resuscitation
options.rationale: Variable decelerations with moderate variability are Category II. Interventions: maternal repositioning, oxygen, IV fluids, amnioinfusion. If worsening, consider operative delivery.

rationale: Category II tracing: resuscitative measures first. If repetitive severe variables with rising baseline or minimal variability → expedite delivery.

question: A 51-year-old G2P2 on postpartum day 3 after C-section presents with fever 39°C, tachycardia, and purulent discharge from the incision site. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: Mastitis presents with breast tenderness, erythema, and fever. This patient's findings are abdominal wall, not breast-related.
Endometritis presents with uterine tenderness, foul lochia, and fever. This patient's primary findings are at the incision, not the uterus.
Post-cesarean fever with localized wound tenderness, erythema, and purulent drainage is a surgical site infection until proven otherwise. Wound culture and broad-spectrum antibiotics are indicated.
UTI causes dysuria, frequency, and suprapubic pain. Without urinary symptoms, wound infection is more likely.

rationale: Post-cesarean wound infection: culture, antibiotics (coverage for MRSA if risk factors), wound opening and drainage if abscess.

question: A 52-year-old primigravida at 41 weeks 5 days with reassuring fetal status and unfavorable cervix (Bishop score 4). What is the most appropriate management?

options.rationale: C-section is not indicated solely for post-term with favorable Bishop score. Induction with cervical ripening is appropriate.
Antenatal testing (BPP or NST) is recommended for post-term pregnancies, but induction at 41+ weeks is still recommended regardless of testing results.
Perinatal risks increase after 41 weeks. Induction at 41 weeks reduces adverse outcomes compared to expectant management until 42 weeks.
Post-term pregnancy (≥41 weeks): induction reduces perinatal mortality and meconium aspiration without increasing C-section rate. Bishop score <6 may require cervical ripening.

rationale: Post-term pregnancy ≥41 weeks: induction recommended with cervical ripening if Bishop <6. Continue fetal surveillance if awaiting spontaneous labor.

question: A 53-year-old at 34 weeks with fundal height measuring 4 weeks behind dates. Ultrasound shows estimated fetal weight <10th percentile with normal amniotic fluid and normal Doppler studies. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: Macrosomia is defined as EFW >90th percentile or >4000 g, the opposite of this scenario.
Amniotic fluid is normal per the scenario. Oligohydramnios would need further evaluation for PROM or placental insufficiency.
SGA with normal fluid and Doppler: likely constitutional or asymmetric growth restriction. Management: serial growth scans, antenatal testing. Normal Dopplers suggest low risk of hypoxia.

options.text: Intrauterine growth restriction from placental insufficiency
options.rationale: Placental insufficiency typically presents with abnormal Dopplers (elevated umbilical artery S/D ratio), oligohydramnios, and asymmetric growth.

rationale: SGA with normal Dopplers and fluid: likely constitutional. IUGR with abnormal Dopplers: closer monitoring, steroids if <34 weeks, deliver for worsening.

question: A 54-year-old at 32 weeks with severe preeclampsia is advised delivery for maternal safety. She refuses C-section due to religious beliefs about surgical delivery. What is the most appropriate course of action?

options.text: Counsel thoroughly, document capacity, explore alternatives, involve ethics committee if needed
options.rationale: A competent patient has the right to refuse treatment. Explore reasons, provide alternatives, document capacity assessment. Ethics committee involvement may help resolve the conflict.
Transfer is an option but does not resolve the underlying ethical conflict. Counseling and multidisciplinary involvement are more appropriate first steps.
Performing surgery without consent constitutes battery. A competent adult's refusal must be respected even if providers disagree.

options.text: Obtain a court order for forced C-section
options.rationale: Court-ordered intervention is reserved for life-threatening emergencies when the patient lacks capacity or in specific jurisdictions for fetal viability. Counseling and alternatives should be exhausted first.

rationale: Competent refusal of C-section: explore concerns, document capacity, involve ethics. Forced surgery is not ethically justified.

question: A 55-year-old at 32 weeks with dichorionic-diamniotic twins presents with preterm labor. Estimated fetal weights are concordant. What is the most appropriate management?

options.rationale: Delivery of one twin in utero is not possible. Both must be delivered together.
Twin pregnancy with preterm labor: tocolysis and steroids as for singletons. DCDA twins have lowest complication risk among twins. Monitor for twin-specific complications.
Selective reduction is performed earlier in pregnancy (first trimester) for higher-order multiples or severe discordance. Not at 32 weeks.
Vaginal delivery is possible for diamniotic twins if presenting twin is cephalic. Immediate delivery is not indicated if fetal status is reassuring.

rationale: Preterm labor in twins: tocolysis + steroids. DCDA twins have the best prognosis. MCDA twins: monitor for TTTS.

question: A 56-year-old presents with 8 weeks amenorrhea, lower abdominal pain, and spotting. BP 100/60, HR 100, adnexal tenderness. Beta-hCG 6000. TVUS shows empty uterus and 2.5 cm adnexal mass with fetal heart activity. What is the most appropriate management?

options.rationale: Expectant management is for low, declining β-hCG with minimal symptoms. This patient has high hCG, cardiac activity, and pain.
MTX candidates: β-hCG <5000, no fetal cardiac activity, mass <3.5 cm, reliable follow-up. This patient has cardiac activity and hCG >5000.
D&C is diagnostic for pregnancy of unknown location, not treatment for ectopic mass. A D&C that shows no villi suggests ectopic pregnancy.
Ectopic pregnancy with β-hCG >5000, visible mass with cardiac activity, or hemodynamic instability: surgical management is indicated. Salpingotomy preserves fertility.

rationale: Ectopic pregnancy: surgical for hCG >5000, cardiac activity, or instability. MTX for unruptured, low hCG, no cardiac activity.

question: A 57-year-old at 10 weeks presents with vaginal bleeding and cramping. On exam, cervical os is open. Products of conception are seen passing through the cervix. What is the most appropriate management?

options.rationale: Medical management is an alternative for incomplete abortion, but surgical evacuation is faster and more predictable when the patient is actively passing tissue.
Ultrasound can confirm retained products but should not delay evacuation when the diagnosis of incomplete abortion is clear on exam.
Prophylactic antibiotics are given before surgical evacuation but are not treatment for incomplete abortion. Tissue must still be removed.
Incomplete abortion with open os and passing tissue: surgical evacuation is definitive and prevents hemorrhage and infection. Expectant management carries higher bleeding risk.

rationale: Incomplete abortion with open cervix and active bleeding: evacuation. Medical management (misoprostol) for incomplete abortion without heavy bleeding.

question: A 58-year-old presents with heavy menstrual bleeding for 6 months, passing clots, flooding, and Hb 8.5 g/dL. Ultrasound shows 3 cm submucosal fibroid. Endometrial biopsy is negative. What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.rationale: Hysterectomy is definitive but reserved for failed medical therapy, completed childbearing, or severe symptoms. Medical management is initial.

options.text: Medical therapy: tranexamic acid + NSAIDs + iron
options.rationale: AUB with fibroid: medical therapy first-line. Tranexamic acid reduces bleeding by 40-50%, NSAIDs reduce pain and bleeding. Iron corrects anemia.
UAE is for symptomatic fibroids after failed medical therapy. It is not first-line treatment for AUB.
Ablation is for AUB without structural causes. Submucosal fibroid is a structural cause that may not be adequately treated by ablation alone.

rationale: AUB with fibroid: medical first-line (TXA, NSAIDs, IUS). Surgical: myomectomy, UAE, or hysterectomy based on fertility wishes and severity.

question: A 59-year-old nulligravida presents with severe cramping pain on day 1-2 of her menses since menarche, limiting daily activity. NSAIDs provide partial relief. Normal physical exam. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: PID presents with vaginal discharge, fever, and cervical motion tenderness, not cyclic menstrual pain since menarche.
Secondary dysmenorrhea develops later in life and suggests underlying pathology (endometriosis, adenomyosis, fibroids). This patient's symptoms began at menarche.
Primary dysmenorrhea begins at or shortly after menarche and is due to prostaglandin-mediated uterine contractions. First-line: NSAIDs + hormonal contraception.
Endometriosis typically presents with chronic pelvic pain, dyspareunia, and infertility. Symptoms starting at menarche without other features favor primary dysmenorrhea.

rationale: Primary dysmenorrhea: NSAIDs + hormonal contraception (COC or IUS). Exercise and heat also helpful.

question: A 60-year-old presents with heavy menses and pelvic pressure. Ultrasound shows a 6 cm intramural fibroid and three smaller fibroids. She desires future fertility. What is the most appropriate management?

options.rationale: UAE is effective for symptom relief but may affect fertility and pregnancy outcomes. Myomectomy is preferred when fertility is desired.
GnRH agonists shrink fibroids but cause hypoestrogenic symptoms and bone loss. Used preoperatively to reduce size or for short-term symptom control.
Symptomatic fibroids in a woman desiring future fertility: myomectomy is the surgical treatment of choice. It removes fibroids while preserving the uterus for pregnancy.
Hysterectomy is definitive but ends fertility. It should not be offered to a patient who desires future pregnancy.

rationale: Symptomatic fibroids with fertility desire: myomectomy. No fertility desire: myomectomy, UAE, or hysterectomy based on patient preference.

question: A 61-year-old is interested in long-term reversible contraception. She has had 2 children, no medical conditions, does not smoke, and wants to space her next pregnancy by 3-5 years. What is the most appropriate method?

options.rationale: COCs are effective but require daily adherence and do not provide the multi-year coverage she seeks. Better for short-term spacing.
Condoms have a 13% typical-use failure rate and are not the most effective option for a patient who wants reliable long-term protection.
LNG-IUS provides highly effective (>99%) long-term contraception for up to 5 years, with the additional benefit of reduced menstrual bleeding. Ideal for spacing.
DMPA is effective for 3 months per injection but requires clinic visits. It may cause weight gain and bone density concerns with long-term use.

rationale: LARC methods (IUD, IUS, implant) are most effective for long-term spacing. LNG-IUS provides non-contraceptive benefits of lighter periods.

question: A 62-year-old nulligravida presents with chronic pelvic pain, deep dyspareunia, and painful periods since age 22. Exam shows tender uterosacral nodules. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: Endometriosis: chronic pelvic pain, dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, tender nodules on exam. Laparoscopy confirms, but clinical diagnosis is often sufficient to start therapy.
Cyst rupture presents with acute severe pain and peritoneal signs. This patient has chronic cyclic symptoms, not acute.
IBS presents with altered bowel habits and abdominal pain related to defecation. It may coexist with endometriosis but does not cause dyspareunia or tender nodules.
PID has acute/subacute onset with fever, discharge, and cervical motion tenderness. Chronic cyclic symptoms since menarche point to endometriosis.

rationale: Endometriosis: NSAIDs + hormonal therapy (COC, progestin, GnRH agonist). Laparoscopic excision for diagnosis and treatment of refractory cases.

question: A 63-year-old presents with lower abdominal pain for 8 months, worse before menses and during intercourse. Exam shows no masses. Ultrasound and laparoscopy are normal. What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.rationale: A single negative laparoscopy with chronic symptoms does not warrant immediate repeat. Conservative management is appropriate.

options.text: Multidisciplinary approach: NSAIDs, COCs, physical therapy, CBT
options.rationale: Chronic pelvic pain with negative workup: multidisciplinary management including medical therapy (NSAIDs, COCs), pelvic floor physical therapy, and cognitive behavioral therapy. Referral to a chronic pain specialist if refractory.
Hysterectomy is not indicated for chronic pelvic pain without identified pathology. Many patients continue to have pain after hysterectomy.
Opioids are not first-line for chronic pelvic pain due to addiction risk and limited efficacy. Multimodal non-opioid management is preferred.

rationale: Chronic pelvic pain: multidisciplinary. Rule out endometriosis, PID, adhesions, GI, and GU causes. Treat underlying cause if identified.

question: A 18-year-old presents with hot flashes, night sweats, vaginal dryness, and insomnia. Last menstrual period was 14 months ago. FSH 85. She has no contraindications. What is the most appropriate management?

options.rationale: Gabapentin reduces hot flash frequency and severity but has side effects (dizziness, drowsiness). It is a second-line non-hormonal option, not first-line.
Vaginal estrogen treats genitourinary syndrome (vaginal dryness, dyspareunia, urinary symptoms) but does not address systemic vasomotor symptoms.
SSRIs/SNRIs are non-hormonal options for women with contraindications to MHT or those who prefer non-hormonal therapy. They are less effective than estrogen for vasomotor symptoms.

options.text: Menopausal hormone therapy (estrogen + progestogen if uterus intact)
options.rationale: MHT is first-line for moderate-to-severe vasomotor symptoms in women <60 or within 10 years of menopause. Estrogen alone if hysterectomy, add progestogen if uterus present to prevent endometrial hyperplasia.

rationale: MHT is most effective for vasomotor symptoms. Lowest effective dose, shortest duration. Risks (breast cancer, VTE) depend on regimen type.

question: A 19-year-old couple presents with 18 months of regular unprotected intercourse without pregnancy. The male partner's semen analysis is normal. What is the most appropriate first test for the female partner?

options.text: Ovulation assessment (mid-luteal progesterone, urine LH kits) + tubal patency (HSG)
options.rationale: Initial female infertility workup: ovulation assessment (progesterone or LH testing) and tubal patency (hysterosalpingogram). Ovarian reserve testing (AMH, FSH) if >35.
Laparoscopy is invasive and not first-line. HSG and ovulation assessment should be done first. Laparoscopy if HSG abnormal or high suspicion.
Infectious serology is part of prepregnancy screening but does not diagnose the cause of infertility.
IVF is third-line after identifying the cause of infertility through basic workup. Most couples do not need IVF.

rationale: Infertility: semen analysis → ovulation → tubal patency. Ovarian reserve if >35. Manage based on identified cause (ovulatory: clomiphene/letrozole; tubal: surgery or IVF).

question: A 20-year-old presents with purulent vaginal discharge, dysuria, and lower abdominal pain. Cervical motion tenderness and adnexal tenderness on exam. Temperature 38.5°C. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: PID: lower abdominal pain, cervical motion tenderness, adnexal tenderness, fever. Caused by ascending infection (Chlamydia, Gonorrhea, anaerobes). Outpatient or inpatient antibiotics based on severity.
BV presents with thin, fishy-smelling discharge without fever or cervical motion tenderness.
Vulvovaginal candidiasis: thick white discharge, pruritus, no fever or cervical motion tenderness.
UTI: dysuria, frequency, suprapubic tenderness, not cervical or adnexal tenderness with fever.

rationale: PID: empiric treatment with ceftriaxone + doxycycline + metronidazole. Treat sexual partners. Screen for HIV and syphilis.

question: A 21-year-old has a Pap smear showing HSIL (high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion). HPV 16 positive. She is otherwise healthy. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.rationale: Hysterectomy is not first-line for CIN 2-3. Cervical conization is sufficient and preserves fertility. Hysterectomy is for recurrent or persistent disease after childbearing.

options.text: Colposcopy with cervical biopsy and endocervical curettage
options.rationale: HSIL (CIN 2-3) on Pap requires colposcopic evaluation with directed biopsies and endocervical sampling to confirm the diagnosis and assess severity before treatment.
LEEP is treatment for confirmed CIN 2-3. Diagnosis must be confirmed by colposcopy and biopsy before proceeding with excisional treatment.
HSIL with high-risk HPV requires immediate colposcopy. Follow-up alone risks progression of CIN 2-3 to invasive cancer.

rationale: HSIL + HPV 16: colposcopy + biopsy → if CIN 2-3 confirmed → excision (LEEP, conization). Annual surveillance after treatment.

question: A 22-year-old presents with abdominal bloating, early satiety, and pelvic pressure. Ultrasound shows a 10 cm complex ovarian cyst with solid components, septations, and ascites. CA-125 is 350. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: Complex ovarian mass with solid components, ascites, and elevated CA-125: highly suspicious for ovarian cancer. Requires surgical staging: total hysterectomy, BSO, omentectomy, and peritoneal biopsies.
Endometriomas appear as homogenous ground-glass echogenicity on ultrasound. They are associated with endometriosis and cause chronic pelvic pain.
Benign cysts are simple (anechoic, thin-walled, no solid components or septations). This mass has complex features highly suggestive of malignancy.
Dermoid cysts contain fat, hair, or calcifications (Rokitansky nodule) and are typically benign. They do not cause markedly elevated CA-125.

rationale: Suspicious ovarian mass: surgical staging (total hysterectomy + BSO + omentectomy + peritoneal biopsies). Neoadjuvant chemo for advanced disease.

question: A 23-year-old at 12 weeks presents with heavy vaginal bleeding and a uterus that is larger than expected for dates. Ultrasound shows a snowstorm pattern without fetal parts. β-hCG is 250,000 IU/L. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: Partial mole has some fetal tissue, lower hCG levels, and focal trophoblastic hyperplasia. Ultrasound may show fetal parts.
Complete mole: no fetal tissue, diffuse trophoblastic proliferation, serum hCG very high (>100,000), snowstorm ultrasound. Management: suction evacuation, serial hCG monitoring.
Choriocarcinoma is a malignant GTD that follows a molar or normal pregnancy. Diagnosed by persistently rising hCG after evacuation.
Multiple gestation shows multiple fetal poles on ultrasound, not a snowstorm pattern. hCG is elevated but not typically >200,000.

rationale: Complete mole: suction evacuation + weekly hCG until undetectable for 3 weeks, then monthly for 6 months. Avoid pregnancy during monitoring.

question: A 24-year-old with obesity and PCOS presents with intermenstrual spotting. Endometrial biopsy shows complex atypical hyperplasia. What is the most appropriate management?

options.rationale: D&C may remove the abnormal tissue temporarily but does not treat the underlying process. Recurrence is expected without definitive treatment.
Progestin therapy is an option for women who desire future fertility. It achieves regression in ~80% but requires close surveillance with repeat biopsies.

options.text: Observation and repeat biopsy in 1 year
options.rationale: Atypical hyperplasia has a high risk of progression to carcinoma. Active treatment (hysterectomy or progestins) is indicated, not observation.
Atypical endometrial hyperplasia has significant risk of concurrent or future endometrial carcinoma. Hysterectomy is definitive treatment for women who have completed childbearing.

rationale: Complex atypical hyperplasia: hysterectomy is definitive. Progestin therapy for fertility preservation with close surveillance.

question: A 25-year-old presents for routine well-woman exam. She has no chronic conditions, BMI 24, no history of fractures, non-smoker. What is the most appropriate recommendation for bone density screening?

options.rationale: The USPSTF and SCFHS recommend DEXA screening for women ≥65. Earlier screening (≥50) is for high-risk women (low BMI, smoking, steroid use, prior fracture, family history).
This patient is below 65 with no risk factors. Early screening is not recommended and may detect incidental low bone density leading to unnecessary treatment.
QCT is not a screening tool for osteoporosis. DEXA is the gold standard with well-established diagnostic criteria (T-score).
Vitamin D testing is not a substitute for bone density screening. It assesses bone health but does not diagnose osteoporosis.

rationale: DEXA screening for women ≥65 or ≥50 with risk factors. T-score ≤-2.5: osteoporosis. Lifestyle + calcium/vitamin D for prevention.

question: A 26-year-old G3P3 presents with a sensation of vaginal bulge and occasional urinary stress incontinence. On exam, the cervix descends to the introitus with Valsalva. What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Pelvic floor physical therapy (Kegel exercises) + behavioral modification
options.rationale: Mild pelvic organ prolapse with stress incontinence: conservative management first-line. Pelvic floor PT, weight loss, avoidance of heavy lifting.
Hysterectomy is indicated for uterine prolapse that is symptomatic and has failed conservative management. Not first-line.
Surgery is for advanced prolapse after conservative measures fail. Not first-line for prolapse at the introitus.
Pessary is an excellent non-surgical option for prolapse but is second-line after PT fails. It provides mechanical support.

rationale: Pelvic organ prolapse: conservative (PT, pessary) first. Surgery for advanced or refractory prolapse. Cystocele/rectocele may require additional repair.

question: A 27-year-old G2P1 with blood type A negative. Her first child was Rh positive. She received RhoGAM after her first delivery. At 28 weeks, antibody screen is negative. What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Routine RhoGAM 300 mcg IM at 28 weeks
options.rationale: Rh-negative woman with negative antibody screen at 28 weeks: RhoGAM prophylaxis is standard to prevent alloimmunization from occult fetomaternal hemorrhage.

options.text: No RhoGAM needed since antibody screen is negative
options.rationale: RhoGAM is given at 28 weeks regardless of negative antibody screen. Without it, occult bleeding can cause sensitization.

options.text: Cordocentesis to determine fetal blood type
options.rationale: Cordocentesis is invasive and not indicated when maternal antibody screen is negative and management is standard.
Antibody screening is repeated at 28 weeks. Monthly screening is not standard. RhoGAM at 28 weeks covers most sensitization risk.

rationale: Rh-negative mother: RhoGAM at 28 weeks and within 72 hours of delivery if baby Rh+. Antibody screen at first visit and 28 weeks.

question: A 28-year-old at 36 weeks reports absent fetal movement for 24 hours. No fetal heart tones are detected. Ultrasound confirms intrauterine fetal death. What is the most appropriate counseling?

options.text: Discuss delivery options, recommend induction, provide emotional support, offer autopsy and genetic testing
options.rationale: IUFD management: deliver the baby (induction or expectant depending on gestational age and maternal safety). Offer evaluation for cause (autopsy, genetic testing, placental pathology). Grief support is essential.
Prolonged retention of a dead fetus risks DIC. Induction is recommended after IUFD is confirmed.

options.text: Emergency C-section to confirm fetal status
options.rationale: C-section is not indicated for confirmed IUFD. Vaginal delivery is safer for the mother. C-section carries surgical risks without fetal benefit.

options.text: Send home with follow-up in 1 week
options.rationale: Management of IUFD requires active planning for delivery. Coagulopathy (DIC) can develop with prolonged retention of dead fetal tissue.

rationale: IUFD: induction or expectant management. Evaluate for cause. DIC risk with prolonged retention. Grief counseling and follow-up.

question: A 29-year-old primigravida with a prolonged second stage of labor (pushing for 3 hours), fetal head at +2 station, occiput anterior. FHR is reassuring. What is the most appropriate management?

options.rationale: Prolonged pushing risks maternal exhaustion, chorioamnionitis, and neonatal morbidity. Intervention is indicated after 3 hours of pushing.
McRoberts is for shoulder dystocia management, not for prolonged second stage without evidence of dystocia.
C-section is indicated for failed operative vaginal delivery, unfavorable station, or non-reassuring fetal status. This patient is a candidate for operative delivery.

Prolonged second stage with reassuring fetal status and favorable station: operative vaginal delivery is appropriate. Vacuum is first-line for OA position. Indications: maternal exhaustion, prolonged pushing, fetal indications.

rationale: Prolonged second stage: operative vaginal delivery if favorable station and position. C-section if vacuum/forceps fails or unfavorable.

question: A 30-year-old presents with hirsutism (Ferriman-Gallwey score 18), acne, oligomenorrhea, and infertility. Testosterone 3.0 (elevated), DHEAS normal, 17-OHP normal. Ultrasound shows polycystic ovaries. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: Cushing: hypercortisolism with central obesity, striae, buffalo hump, proximal weakness. This patient has hyperandrogenism without cortisol excess.
PCOS: hyperandrogenism (clinical or biochemical), oligo/anovulation, polycystic ovaries (2 of 3 criteria). Elevated testosterone with normal DHEAS and 17-OHP excludes adrenal causes.
Non-classic CAH due to 21-hydroxylase deficiency presents with elevated 17-OHP. This patient's 17-OHP is normal, excluding the diagnosis.
Adrenal tumors produce DHEAS and/or cortisol. Normal DHEAS excludes an adrenal source of androgen excess in most cases.

rationale: PCOS: Rotterdam criteria (2 of 3). Management: COCs for hirsutism, metformin/letrozole for fertility, lifestyle modification for metabolic health.

question: A 31-year-old at 6 weeks with a wanted pregnancy is found to have missed abortion on ultrasound. She is hemodynamically stable. She requests "natural management" and does not want surgical intervention. What is the most appropriate counseling?

options.rationale: Surgical evacuation is the most predictable approach but is not mandatory. Expectant and medical management are valid options when the patient is stable.

options.text: Present all options: expectant, medical (misoprostol), or surgical. Support her decision after informed consent
options.rationale: Missed abortion management includes expectant (1-4 weeks for spontaneous passage), medical (misoprostol), or surgical (D&C). The patient's autonomy should be respected after counseling on risks/benefits of each.
Methotrexate is for ectopic pregnancy, not missed abortion. Misoprostol is the appropriate medical agent for early pregnancy loss.
Ethics committee referral is not needed for standard management of early pregnancy loss. All management options are medically and ethically acceptable.

rationale: Missed abortion: offer all three options (expectant, medical, surgical). Respect patient autonomy while ensuring informed decision-making.

question: A 32-year-old asks about cervical cancer screening. She is healthy, non-smoker, no prior abnormal Paps. What is the most appropriate screening recommendation?

options.text: Pap smear every 3 years starting at age 21, or co-testing (Pap + HPV) every 5 years starting at age 30
options.rationale: Cervical screening: age 21-29: Pap every 3 years. Age 30-65: Pap + HPV co-testing every 5 years or Pap alone every 3 years.

options.text: HPV vaccine only, no Pap needed
options.rationale: HPV vaccine prevents HPV types 16/18 (causing 70% of cervical cancers) but does not eliminate the need for screening as other high-risk types exist.

options.text: Pap smear every year starting at age 18
options.rationale: Annual screening is not recommended. Screening starts at 21 regardless of sexual activity. Over-screening can lead to unnecessary procedures.
Cervical cancer screening is recommended for all women 21-65 regardless of symptoms. Precancerous lesions are asymptomatic.

rationale: Cervical cancer screening: Pap 3-yearly ages 21-29, co-test 5-yearly ages 30-65. Stop at 65 with adequate prior negative screens.

question: A 33-year-old at 20 weeks presents with a 2 cm firm breast mass that she noticed 2 weeks ago. Ultrasound shows a solid, irregular mass. What is the most appropriate diagnostic approach?

options.rationale: Mammogram can be performed safely in pregnancy with abdominal shielding but is adjunctive to ultrasound and biopsy, not a replacement.
Any suspicious breast mass in pregnancy requires definitive diagnosis without delay. Breast cancer aggressiveness is similar in pregnancy.
A solid, irregular breast mass in pregnancy requires tissue diagnosis. Core needle biopsy is safe during pregnancy and is the gold standard for diagnosis.
MRI with contrast has limited safety data in pregnancy and is not first-line for evaluating breast masses. Ultrasound + biopsy is preferred.

rationale: Suspicious breast mass in pregnancy: ultrasound + core needle biopsy. Mammogram with shielding is safe. Cancer treatment depends on gestational age.

question: A 34-year-old primigravida at 34 weeks presents with BP 160/105, proteinuria 3+, and severe headache. Platelets 90, ALT 120, Cr 1.2. What is the most appropriate management?

options.rationale: Severe preeclampsia with end-organ damage precludes expectant management. Delaying delivery risks eclampsia, hepatic rupture, and maternal death.
Severe preeclampsia requires inpatient management with IV antihypertensives and monitoring. Outpatient care is for mild disease only.
MgSO4 is for seizure prophylaxis, not treatment of underlying disease. Delivery remains the definitive management.

options.text: Deliver after corticosteroid course if stable
options.rationale: Severe preeclampsia at ≥34 weeks requires delivery. A short course of steroids for fetal lung maturity can be given if maternal and fetal status permit delay.

rationale: Severe preeclampsia ≥34 weeks: deliver after steroids. MgSO4 for seizure prophylaxis. BP control with labetalol or hydralazine.

question: A 35-year-old at 32 weeks presents with painless bright red vaginal bleeding. No contractions. Fundal height appropriate. What is the most appropriate initial diagnostic step?

options.rationale: Digital exam is contraindicated when previa is suspected due to risk of provoking catastrophic hemorrhage.
BPP assesses fetal wellbeing but does not diagnose the cause of bleeding. Placental localization is the priority.
Painless third trimester bleeding is placenta previa until proven otherwise. Ultrasound is first-line and safe. Digital exam is contraindicated.

options.text: Amniocentesis to assess fetal lung maturity
options.rationale: Amniocentesis has no role in diagnosing the cause of acute third-trimester bleeding and carries procedural risk.

rationale: Painless third trimester bleeding: ultrasound to locate placenta. NO digital exam. If previa confirmed: admit, steroids, deliver at 36-37 weeks if stable.

question: A 36-year-old at 36 weeks presents with sudden severe abdominal pain and dark vaginal bleeding. Uterus is rigid and tender. FHR shows late decelerations. BP 85/50. What is the most appropriate management?

options.rationale: Fetal distress and maternal instability mandate immediate delivery. Expectant management risks fetal death and maternal coagulopathy.
Abruption is a clinical diagnosis. Delaying delivery for imaging risks fetal demise.
Tocolysis is contraindicated in abruption. Uterine contractions may worsen bleeding and fetal compromise.
Abruption with non-reassuring fetal status and maternal hemodynamic instability requires emergency delivery. DIC is a life-threatening complication.

rationale: Abruptio placentae with fetal distress and maternal shock: emergency delivery. Evaluate for DIC and prepare for massive transfusion.

question: A 37-year-old at 30 weeks presents with regular painful contractions and cervical dilation of 3 cm on exam. Membranes intact. Fetal status reassuring. What is the most appropriate management?

options.rationale: Preterm labor requires hospitalization for monitoring, tocolysis, and steroid administration. Outpatient management is not appropriate.
Delivery is indicated when tocolysis is contraindicated (chorioamnionitis, severe preeclampsia, non-reassuring fetal status) or labor is too advanced.
Tocolysis buys time for steroids to work (maximal effect at 48 hours). With 3 cm dilation, the patient may deliver before steroids take effect without tocolysis.
Preterm labor at <34 weeks with intact membranes and reassuring fetal status: tocolysis for 48 hours allows corticosteroids to enhance fetal lung maturity.

rationale: Preterm labor <34 weeks: tocolysis + steroids + GBS prophylaxis. If cervical dilation >6 cm or chorioamnionitis: deliver.

question: A 38-year-old at 36 weeks presents with fluid leaking per vagina for 2 hours. Pooling and ferning are positive on speculum exam. No contractions. Fetal status reassuring. What is the most appropriate management?

options.rationale: PROM at ≥36 weeks: induction of labor is recommended to reduce chorioamnionitis risk. GBS prophylaxis should be given if indicated.
There is no surgical method to reseal ruptured membranes. Induction or expectant management are the only options.
Tocolysis is contraindicated in PROM due to infection risk. Delivery is the goal when the cervix is unfavorable and membranes are ruptured at term.
PROM at ≤37 weeks is managed by induction unless very close to term. The risk of ascending infection outweighs benefits of waiting.

rationale: PROM ≥36 weeks: induction. 34-36 weeks: steroids + induction vs expectant. <34 weeks: steroids + antibiotics + expectant management with monitoring for infection.

question: A 39-year-old delivered vaginally 20 minutes ago. Fundus is boggy and uterus is at the umbilicus. Heavy bright red bleeding continues despite fundal massage. What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacologic management?

options.text: IV oxytocin 10-40 IU in 1 L normal saline
options.rationale: Oxytocin is first-line for uterine atony. It causes sustained uterine contraction. Dose: 10-40 IU in 1 L NS, infused at 125-200 mL/hour.
Misoprostol is third-line and less effective than oxytocin. Used when IV access is limited. Causes fever and shivering.
Carboprost (PGF2α) is second-line when oxytocin fails. Contraindicated in asthma. Effective for atony but causes nausea, vomiting, and bronchospasm.
TXA 1 g IV is adjunctive, given within 3 hours of delivery. It reduces death from bleeding by 20% but does not replace uterotonics.

rationale: PPH: uterine massage + oxytocin first-line. Escalate: ergometrine → carboprost → misoprostol → intrauterine balloon → surgical.

question: A 40-year-old at 28 weeks has a hemoglobin of 10.2 g/dL. MCV 82, ferritin 15. Which physiologic change of pregnancy most likely contributes to this finding?

options.rationale: Fetal iron demands increase in the third trimester, but physiologic hemodilution is the primary cause of lower hemoglobin earlier. Iron studies help distinguish.

options.text: Physiologic hemodilution from plasma volume expansion
options.rationale: Plasma volume increases ~50% while red cell mass increases only ~25%, causing dilutional anemia in the second and third trimesters. This is physiologic, not pathologic.
Folate deficiency causes macrocytic anemia (high MCV). This patient's MCV is normal, making folate deficiency unlikely.
Pregnancy does not cause hemolysis. A falling hemoglobin with elevated LDH and low haptoglobin would suggest pathologic hemolysis.

rationale: Gestational anemia is primarily dilutional. Iron, folate, and B12 should be evaluated. Supplementation is standard regardless.

question: A 41-year-old primigravida at 10 weeks presents for initial prenatal visit. She is healthy with no chronic conditions. What routine lab tests should be ordered at this visit?

options.rationale: Chest X-ray is not a routine prenatal lab. TB screening is indicated only for high-risk populations (exposure, symptoms, high-prevalence country).

options.text: OGTT for gestational diabetes at 10 weeks
options.rationale: OGTT is performed at 24-28 weeks routinely or earlier only if risk factors (prior GDM, BMI >30). Not part of initial visit labs.

options.text: Blood type/Rh, antibody screen, CBC, HIV, syphilis, hepatitis B, rubella titer, urinalysis
options.rationale: Standard first-trimester labs include blood group + antibody screen, CBC, HIV, syphilis, HBsAg, rubella, and urinalysis. These establish baseline and identify risks.
Amniocentesis is offered at 15-20 weeks for women ≥35 or abnormal NIPT/serum screen. Not routine at 10 weeks.

rationale: First prenatal visit: comprehensive history, blood work, urinalysis, dating ultrasound. Supplements: folic acid, iron, vitamin D.

question: A 42-year-old primigravida at 40 weeks presents with contractions every 3 minutes, cervical dilation 6 cm, 100% effaced. FHR is 145 with moderate variability. What stage of labor is this patient in?

options.rationale: Second stage begins at complete dilation (10 cm) and ends with delivery. This patient is not yet fully dilated.
Latent phase: 0-6 cm, slower progress. This patient has passed the latent-to-active transition at 6 cm.
Active first stage: 6-10 cm dilation, regular contractions. Nulliparous women dilate ~1 cm/hour. FHR monitoring should be continuous.
Third stage is from delivery of the infant to delivery of the placenta. This patient is still in the active phase of first stage.

rationale: Active phase (6-10 cm) progresses at ~1 cm/hour for nulliparas. If protraction or arrest occurs, evaluate for augmentation with oxytocin.

question: A 43-year-old G1P1 had a vaginal delivery with second-degree perineal laceration repaired. She is breastfeeding. Which contraceptive method is most appropriate at this postpartum visit?

options.rationale: Tubal ligation is permanent and requires informed consent before or after delivery. It is not the first-line recommendation for a healthy new mother.
Natural family planning has high failure rates in the postpartum period due to unpredictable return of ovulation and cycles.

options.text: Progestin-only pill or IUD (Cu-IUD or LNG-IUS)
options.rationale: Postpartum contraception: progestin-only methods and IUDs are safe during breastfeeding. Progestin-only pills start immediately; IUDs can be placed at 4-6 weeks postpartum.
COCs are relatively contraindicated during breastfeeding in the first 3-6 weeks due to potential effects on milk production. Progestin-only methods are preferred.

rationale: Postpartum contraception: progestin-only methods are safe during breastfeeding. IUDs placed at 4-6 weeks postpartum.

question: A 44-year-old at 39 weeks in active labor has an FHR tracing showing variable decelerations dropping to 70 bpm, lasting 60 seconds, with moderate variability between contractions. What is the most appropriate interpretation?

options.rationale: Category III: absent variability + recurrent late/variables, or bradycardia. This has moderate variability, making it Category II.

options.text: Category II (indeterminate) — continue monitoring and consider intrauterine resuscitation
options.rationale: Variable decelerations with moderate variability are Category II. Interventions: maternal repositioning, oxygen, IV fluids, amnioinfusion. If worsening, consider operative delivery.
Fetal scalp sampling is used to clarify indeterminate tracings but is not the first step. Intrauterine resuscitation should be initiated first.
Category I requires all: baseline 110-160, moderate variability, NO decelerations. Variables make this Category II.

rationale: Category II tracing: resuscitative measures first. If repetitive severe variables with rising baseline or minimal variability → expedite delivery.

question: A 45-year-old G2P2 on postpartum day 3 after C-section presents with fever 39°C, tachycardia, and purulent discharge from the incision site. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: Post-cesarean fever with localized wound tenderness, erythema, and purulent drainage is a surgical site infection until proven otherwise. Wound culture and broad-spectrum antibiotics are indicated.
Mastitis presents with breast tenderness, erythema, and fever. This patient's findings are abdominal wall, not breast-related.
Endometritis presents with uterine tenderness, foul lochia, and fever. This patient's primary findings are at the incision, not the uterus.
UTI causes dysuria, frequency, and suprapubic pain. Without urinary symptoms, wound infection is more likely.

rationale: Post-cesarean wound infection: culture, antibiotics (coverage for MRSA if risk factors), wound opening and drainage if abscess.

question: A 46-year-old primigravida at 41 weeks 5 days with reassuring fetal status and unfavorable cervix (Bishop score 4). What is the most appropriate management?

options.rationale: C-section is not indicated solely for post-term with favorable Bishop score. Induction with cervical ripening is appropriate.
Antenatal testing (BPP or NST) is recommended for post-term pregnancies, but induction at 41+ weeks is still recommended regardless of testing results.
Perinatal risks increase after 41 weeks. Induction at 41 weeks reduces adverse outcomes compared to expectant management until 42 weeks.
Post-term pregnancy (≥41 weeks): induction reduces perinatal mortality and meconium aspiration without increasing C-section rate. Bishop score <6 may require cervical ripening.

rationale: Post-term pregnancy ≥41 weeks: induction recommended with cervical ripening if Bishop <6. Continue fetal surveillance if awaiting spontaneous labor.

question: A 47-year-old at 34 weeks with fundal height measuring 4 weeks behind dates. Ultrasound shows estimated fetal weight <10th percentile with normal amniotic fluid and normal Doppler studies. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Intrauterine growth restriction from placental insufficiency
options.rationale: Placental insufficiency typically presents with abnormal Dopplers (elevated umbilical artery S/D ratio), oligohydramnios, and asymmetric growth.
Macrosomia is defined as EFW >90th percentile or >4000 g, the opposite of this scenario.
Amniotic fluid is normal per the scenario. Oligohydramnios would need further evaluation for PROM or placental insufficiency.
SGA with normal fluid and Doppler: likely constitutional or asymmetric growth restriction. Management: serial growth scans, antenatal testing. Normal Dopplers suggest low risk of hypoxia.

rationale: SGA with normal Dopplers and fluid: likely constitutional. IUGR with abnormal Dopplers: closer monitoring, steroids if <34 weeks, deliver for worsening.

question: A 48-year-old at 32 weeks with severe preeclampsia is advised delivery for maternal safety. She refuses C-section due to religious beliefs about surgical delivery. What is the most appropriate course of action?

options.text: Obtain a court order for forced C-section
options.rationale: Court-ordered intervention is reserved for life-threatening emergencies when the patient lacks capacity or in specific jurisdictions for fetal viability. Counseling and alternatives should be exhausted first.
Performing surgery without consent constitutes battery. A competent adult's refusal must be respected even if providers disagree.

options.text: Counsel thoroughly, document capacity, explore alternatives, involve ethics committee if needed
options.rationale: A competent patient has the right to refuse treatment. Explore reasons, provide alternatives, document capacity assessment. Ethics committee involvement may help resolve the conflict.
Transfer is an option but does not resolve the underlying ethical conflict. Counseling and multidisciplinary involvement are more appropriate first steps.

rationale: Competent refusal of C-section: explore concerns, document capacity, involve ethics. Forced surgery is not ethically justified.

question: A 49-year-old at 32 weeks with dichorionic-diamniotic twins presents with preterm labor. Estimated fetal weights are concordant. What is the most appropriate management?

options.rationale: Twin pregnancy with preterm labor: tocolysis and steroids as for singletons. DCDA twins have lowest complication risk among twins. Monitor for twin-specific complications.
Vaginal delivery is possible for diamniotic twins if presenting twin is cephalic. Immediate delivery is not indicated if fetal status is reassuring.
Delivery of one twin in utero is not possible. Both must be delivered together.
Selective reduction is performed earlier in pregnancy (first trimester) for higher-order multiples or severe discordance. Not at 32 weeks.

rationale: Preterm labor in twins: tocolysis + steroids. DCDA twins have the best prognosis. MCDA twins: monitor for TTTS.

question: A 50-year-old presents with 8 weeks amenorrhea, lower abdominal pain, and spotting. BP 100/60, HR 100, adnexal tenderness. Beta-hCG 6000. TVUS shows empty uterus and 2.5 cm adnexal mass with fetal heart activity. What is the most appropriate management?

options.rationale: Ectopic pregnancy with β-hCG >5000, visible mass with cardiac activity, or hemodynamic instability: surgical management is indicated. Salpingotomy preserves fertility.
D&C is diagnostic for pregnancy of unknown location, not treatment for ectopic mass. A D&C that shows no villi suggests ectopic pregnancy.
MTX candidates: β-hCG <5000, no fetal cardiac activity, mass <3.5 cm, reliable follow-up. This patient has cardiac activity and hCG >5000.
Expectant management is for low, declining β-hCG with minimal symptoms. This patient has high hCG, cardiac activity, and pain.

rationale: Ectopic pregnancy: surgical for hCG >5000, cardiac activity, or instability. MTX for unruptured, low hCG, no cardiac activity.

question: A 51-year-old at 10 weeks presents with vaginal bleeding and cramping. On exam, cervical os is open. Products of conception are seen passing through the cervix. What is the most appropriate management?

options.rationale: Ultrasound can confirm retained products but should not delay evacuation when the diagnosis of incomplete abortion is clear on exam.
Medical management is an alternative for incomplete abortion, but surgical evacuation is faster and more predictable when the patient is actively passing tissue.
Incomplete abortion with open os and passing tissue: surgical evacuation is definitive and prevents hemorrhage and infection. Expectant management carries higher bleeding risk.
Prophylactic antibiotics are given before surgical evacuation but are not treatment for incomplete abortion. Tissue must still be removed.

rationale: Incomplete abortion with open cervix and active bleeding: evacuation. Medical management (misoprostol) for incomplete abortion without heavy bleeding.

question: A 52-year-old presents with heavy menstrual bleeding for 6 months, passing clots, flooding, and Hb 8.5 g/dL. Ultrasound shows 3 cm submucosal fibroid. Endometrial biopsy is negative. What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.rationale: Hysterectomy is definitive but reserved for failed medical therapy, completed childbearing, or severe symptoms. Medical management is initial.
UAE is for symptomatic fibroids after failed medical therapy. It is not first-line treatment for AUB.
Ablation is for AUB without structural causes. Submucosal fibroid is a structural cause that may not be adequately treated by ablation alone.

options.text: Medical therapy: tranexamic acid + NSAIDs + iron
options.rationale: AUB with fibroid: medical therapy first-line. Tranexamic acid reduces bleeding by 40-50%, NSAIDs reduce pain and bleeding. Iron corrects anemia.

rationale: AUB with fibroid: medical first-line (TXA, NSAIDs, IUS). Surgical: myomectomy, UAE, or hysterectomy based on fertility wishes and severity.

question: A 53-year-old nulligravida presents with severe cramping pain on day 1-2 of her menses since menarche, limiting daily activity. NSAIDs provide partial relief. Normal physical exam. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: PID presents with vaginal discharge, fever, and cervical motion tenderness, not cyclic menstrual pain since menarche.
Secondary dysmenorrhea develops later in life and suggests underlying pathology (endometriosis, adenomyosis, fibroids). This patient's symptoms began at menarche.
Primary dysmenorrhea begins at or shortly after menarche and is due to prostaglandin-mediated uterine contractions. First-line: NSAIDs + hormonal contraception.
Endometriosis typically presents with chronic pelvic pain, dyspareunia, and infertility. Symptoms starting at menarche without other features favor primary dysmenorrhea.

rationale: Primary dysmenorrhea: NSAIDs + hormonal contraception (COC or IUS). Exercise and heat also helpful.

question: A 54-year-old presents with heavy menses and pelvic pressure. Ultrasound shows a 6 cm intramural fibroid and three smaller fibroids. She desires future fertility. What is the most appropriate management?

options.rationale: UAE is effective for symptom relief but may affect fertility and pregnancy outcomes. Myomectomy is preferred when fertility is desired.
GnRH agonists shrink fibroids but cause hypoestrogenic symptoms and bone loss. Used preoperatively to reduce size or for short-term symptom control.
Symptomatic fibroids in a woman desiring future fertility: myomectomy is the surgical treatment of choice. It removes fibroids while preserving the uterus for pregnancy.
Hysterectomy is definitive but ends fertility. It should not be offered to a patient who desires future pregnancy.

rationale: Symptomatic fibroids with fertility desire: myomectomy. No fertility desire: myomectomy, UAE, or hysterectomy based on patient preference.

question: A 55-year-old is interested in long-term reversible contraception. She has had 2 children, no medical conditions, does not smoke, and wants to space her next pregnancy by 3-5 years. What is the most appropriate method?

options.rationale: Condoms have a 13% typical-use failure rate and are not the most effective option for a patient who wants reliable long-term protection.
COCs are effective but require daily adherence and do not provide the multi-year coverage she seeks. Better for short-term spacing.
LNG-IUS provides highly effective (>99%) long-term contraception for up to 5 years, with the additional benefit of reduced menstrual bleeding. Ideal for spacing.
DMPA is effective for 3 months per injection but requires clinic visits. It may cause weight gain and bone density concerns with long-term use.

rationale: LARC methods (IUD, IUS, implant) are most effective for long-term spacing. LNG-IUS provides non-contraceptive benefits of lighter periods.

question: A 56-year-old nulligravida presents with chronic pelvic pain, deep dyspareunia, and painful periods since age 22. Exam shows tender uterosacral nodules. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: IBS presents with altered bowel habits and abdominal pain related to defecation. It may coexist with endometriosis but does not cause dyspareunia or tender nodules.
Cyst rupture presents with acute severe pain and peritoneal signs. This patient has chronic cyclic symptoms, not acute.
PID has acute/subacute onset with fever, discharge, and cervical motion tenderness. Chronic cyclic symptoms since menarche point to endometriosis.
Endometriosis: chronic pelvic pain, dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, tender nodules on exam. Laparoscopy confirms, but clinical diagnosis is often sufficient to start therapy.

rationale: Endometriosis: NSAIDs + hormonal therapy (COC, progestin, GnRH agonist). Laparoscopic excision for diagnosis and treatment of refractory cases.

question: A 57-year-old presents with lower abdominal pain for 8 months, worse before menses and during intercourse. Exam shows no masses. Ultrasound and laparoscopy are normal. What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.rationale: Opioids are not first-line for chronic pelvic pain due to addiction risk and limited efficacy. Multimodal non-opioid management is preferred.
Hysterectomy is not indicated for chronic pelvic pain without identified pathology. Many patients continue to have pain after hysterectomy.

options.text: Multidisciplinary approach: NSAIDs, COCs, physical therapy, CBT
options.rationale: Chronic pelvic pain with negative workup: multidisciplinary management including medical therapy (NSAIDs, COCs), pelvic floor physical therapy, and cognitive behavioral therapy. Referral to a chronic pain specialist if refractory.
A single negative laparoscopy with chronic symptoms does not warrant immediate repeat. Conservative management is appropriate.

rationale: Chronic pelvic pain: multidisciplinary. Rule out endometriosis, PID, adhesions, GI, and GU causes. Treat underlying cause if identified.

question: A 58-year-old presents with hot flashes, night sweats, vaginal dryness, and insomnia. Last menstrual period was 14 months ago. FSH 85. She has no contraindications. What is the most appropriate management?

options.rationale: SSRIs/SNRIs are non-hormonal options for women with contraindications to MHT or those who prefer non-hormonal therapy. They are less effective than estrogen for vasomotor symptoms.
Gabapentin reduces hot flash frequency and severity but has side effects (dizziness, drowsiness). It is a second-line non-hormonal option, not first-line.

options.text: Menopausal hormone therapy (estrogen + progestogen if uterus intact)
options.rationale: MHT is first-line for moderate-to-severe vasomotor symptoms in women <60 or within 10 years of menopause. Estrogen alone if hysterectomy, add progestogen if uterus present to prevent endometrial hyperplasia.
Vaginal estrogen treats genitourinary syndrome (vaginal dryness, dyspareunia, urinary symptoms) but does not address systemic vasomotor symptoms.

rationale: MHT is most effective for vasomotor symptoms. Lowest effective dose, shortest duration. Risks (breast cancer, VTE) depend on regimen type.

question: A 59-year-old couple presents with 18 months of regular unprotected intercourse without pregnancy. The male partner's semen analysis is normal. What is the most appropriate first test for the female partner?

options.rationale: Laparoscopy is invasive and not first-line. HSG and ovulation assessment should be done first. Laparoscopy if HSG abnormal or high suspicion.

options.text: Ovulation assessment (mid-luteal progesterone, urine LH kits) + tubal patency (HSG)
options.rationale: Initial female infertility workup: ovulation assessment (progesterone or LH testing) and tubal patency (hysterosalpingogram). Ovarian reserve testing (AMH, FSH) if >35.
Infectious serology is part of prepregnancy screening but does not diagnose the cause of infertility.
IVF is third-line after identifying the cause of infertility through basic workup. Most couples do not need IVF.

rationale: Infertility: semen analysis → ovulation → tubal patency. Ovarian reserve if >35. Manage based on identified cause (ovulatory: clomiphene/letrozole; tubal: surgery or IVF).

question: A 60-year-old presents with purulent vaginal discharge, dysuria, and lower abdominal pain. Cervical motion tenderness and adnexal tenderness on exam. Temperature 38.5°C. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: Vulvovaginal candidiasis: thick white discharge, pruritus, no fever or cervical motion tenderness.
UTI: dysuria, frequency, suprapubic tenderness, not cervical or adnexal tenderness with fever.
BV presents with thin, fishy-smelling discharge without fever or cervical motion tenderness.

PID: lower abdominal pain, cervical motion tenderness, adnexal tenderness, fever. Caused by ascending infection (Chlamydia, Gonorrhea, anaerobes). Outpatient or inpatient antibiotics based on severity.

rationale: PID: empiric treatment with ceftriaxone + doxycycline + metronidazole. Treat sexual partners. Screen for HIV and syphilis.

question: A 61-year-old has a Pap smear showing HSIL (high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion). HPV 16 positive. She is otherwise healthy. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Colposcopy with cervical biopsy and endocervical curettage
options.rationale: HSIL (CIN 2-3) on Pap requires colposcopic evaluation with directed biopsies and endocervical sampling to confirm the diagnosis and assess severity before treatment.
LEEP is treatment for confirmed CIN 2-3. Diagnosis must be confirmed by colposcopy and biopsy before proceeding with excisional treatment.
Hysterectomy is not first-line for CIN 2-3. Cervical conization is sufficient and preserves fertility. Hysterectomy is for recurrent or persistent disease after childbearing.
HSIL with high-risk HPV requires immediate colposcopy. Follow-up alone risks progression of CIN 2-3 to invasive cancer.

rationale: HSIL + HPV 16: colposcopy + biopsy → if CIN 2-3 confirmed → excision (LEEP, conization). Annual surveillance after treatment.

question: A 62-year-old presents with abdominal bloating, early satiety, and pelvic pressure. Ultrasound shows a 10 cm complex ovarian cyst with solid components, septations, and ascites. CA-125 is 350. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: Dermoid cysts contain fat, hair, or calcifications (Rokitansky nodule) and are typically benign. They do not cause markedly elevated CA-125.
Benign cysts are simple (anechoic, thin-walled, no solid components or septations). This mass has complex features highly suggestive of malignancy.

Complex ovarian mass with solid components, ascites, and elevated CA-125: highly suspicious for ovarian cancer. Requires surgical staging: total hysterectomy, BSO, omentectomy, and peritoneal biopsies.
Endometriomas appear as homogenous ground-glass echogenicity on ultrasound. They are associated with endometriosis and cause chronic pelvic pain.

rationale: Suspicious ovarian mass: surgical staging (total hysterectomy + BSO + omentectomy + peritoneal biopsies). Neoadjuvant chemo for advanced disease.

question: A 63-year-old at 12 weeks presents with heavy vaginal bleeding and a uterus that is larger than expected for dates. Ultrasound shows a snowstorm pattern without fetal parts. β-hCG is 250,000 IU/L. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: Complete mole: no fetal tissue, diffuse trophoblastic proliferation, serum hCG very high (>100,000), snowstorm ultrasound. Management: suction evacuation, serial hCG monitoring.
Partial mole has some fetal tissue, lower hCG levels, and focal trophoblastic hyperplasia. Ultrasound may show fetal parts.
Multiple gestation shows multiple fetal poles on ultrasound, not a snowstorm pattern. hCG is elevated but not typically >200,000.
Choriocarcinoma is a malignant GTD that follows a molar or normal pregnancy. Diagnosed by persistently rising hCG after evacuation.

rationale: Complete mole: suction evacuation + weekly hCG until undetectable for 3 weeks, then monthly for 6 months. Avoid pregnancy during monitoring.

question: A 18-year-old with obesity and PCOS presents with intermenstrual spotting. Endometrial biopsy shows complex atypical hyperplasia. What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Observation and repeat biopsy in 1 year
options.rationale: Atypical hyperplasia has a high risk of progression to carcinoma. Active treatment (hysterectomy or progestins) is indicated, not observation.
Atypical endometrial hyperplasia has significant risk of concurrent or future endometrial carcinoma. Hysterectomy is definitive treatment for women who have completed childbearing.
D&C may remove the abnormal tissue temporarily but does not treat the underlying process. Recurrence is expected without definitive treatment.
Progestin therapy is an option for women who desire future fertility. It achieves regression in ~80% but requires close surveillance with repeat biopsies.

rationale: Complex atypical hyperplasia: hysterectomy is definitive. Progestin therapy for fertility preservation with close surveillance.

question: A 19-year-old presents for routine well-woman exam. She has no chronic conditions, BMI 24, no history of fractures, non-smoker. What is the most appropriate recommendation for bone density screening?

options.rationale: The USPSTF and SCFHS recommend DEXA screening for women ≥65. Earlier screening (≥50) is for high-risk women (low BMI, smoking, steroid use, prior fracture, family history).
This patient is below 65 with no risk factors. Early screening is not recommended and may detect incidental low bone density leading to unnecessary treatment.
Vitamin D testing is not a substitute for bone density screening. It assesses bone health but does not diagnose osteoporosis.
QCT is not a screening tool for osteoporosis. DEXA is the gold standard with well-established diagnostic criteria (T-score).

rationale: DEXA screening for women ≥65 or ≥50 with risk factors. T-score ≤-2.5: osteoporosis. Lifestyle + calcium/vitamin D for prevention.

question: A 20-year-old G3P3 presents with a sensation of vaginal bulge and occasional urinary stress incontinence. On exam, the cervix descends to the introitus with Valsalva. What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.rationale: Pessary is an excellent non-surgical option for prolapse but is second-line after PT fails. It provides mechanical support.
Hysterectomy is indicated for uterine prolapse that is symptomatic and has failed conservative management. Not first-line.
Surgery is for advanced prolapse after conservative measures fail. Not first-line for prolapse at the introitus.

options.text: Pelvic floor physical therapy (Kegel exercises) + behavioral modification
options.rationale: Mild pelvic organ prolapse with stress incontinence: conservative management first-line. Pelvic floor PT, weight loss, avoidance of heavy lifting.

rationale: Pelvic organ prolapse: conservative (PT, pessary) first. Surgery for advanced or refractory prolapse. Cystocele/rectocele may require additional repair.

question: A 21-year-old G2P1 with blood type A negative. Her first child was Rh positive. She received RhoGAM after her first delivery. At 28 weeks, antibody screen is negative. What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: No RhoGAM needed since antibody screen is negative
options.rationale: RhoGAM is given at 28 weeks regardless of negative antibody screen. Without it, occult bleeding can cause sensitization.
Antibody screening is repeated at 28 weeks. Monthly screening is not standard. RhoGAM at 28 weeks covers most sensitization risk.

options.text: Cordocentesis to determine fetal blood type
options.rationale: Cordocentesis is invasive and not indicated when maternal antibody screen is negative and management is standard.

options.text: Routine RhoGAM 300 mcg IM at 28 weeks
options.rationale: Rh-negative woman with negative antibody screen at 28 weeks: RhoGAM prophylaxis is standard to prevent alloimmunization from occult fetomaternal hemorrhage.

rationale: Rh-negative mother: RhoGAM at 28 weeks and within 72 hours of delivery if baby Rh+. Antibody screen at first visit and 28 weeks.

question: A 22-year-old at 36 weeks reports absent fetal movement for 24 hours. No fetal heart tones are detected. Ultrasound confirms intrauterine fetal death. What is the most appropriate counseling?

options.text: Discuss delivery options, recommend induction, provide emotional support, offer autopsy and genetic testing
options.rationale: IUFD management: deliver the baby (induction or expectant depending on gestational age and maternal safety). Offer evaluation for cause (autopsy, genetic testing, placental pathology). Grief support is essential.

options.text: Emergency C-section to confirm fetal status
options.rationale: C-section is not indicated for confirmed IUFD. Vaginal delivery is safer for the mother. C-section carries surgical risks without fetal benefit.
Prolonged retention of a dead fetus risks DIC. Induction is recommended after IUFD is confirmed.

options.text: Send home with follow-up in 1 week
options.rationale: Management of IUFD requires active planning for delivery. Coagulopathy (DIC) can develop with prolonged retention of dead fetal tissue.

rationale: IUFD: induction or expectant management. Evaluate for cause. DIC risk with prolonged retention. Grief counseling and follow-up.

question: A 23-year-old primigravida with a prolonged second stage of labor (pushing for 3 hours), fetal head at +2 station, occiput anterior. FHR is reassuring. What is the most appropriate management?

options.rationale: Prolonged pushing risks maternal exhaustion, chorioamnionitis, and neonatal morbidity. Intervention is indicated after 3 hours of pushing.
McRoberts is for shoulder dystocia management, not for prolonged second stage without evidence of dystocia.

Prolonged second stage with reassuring fetal status and favorable station: operative vaginal delivery is appropriate. Vacuum is first-line for OA position. Indications: maternal exhaustion, prolonged pushing, fetal indications.
C-section is indicated for failed operative vaginal delivery, unfavorable station, or non-reassuring fetal status. This patient is a candidate for operative delivery.
